                                      v
                              Local evaluator
                                      |
                           flag value + reason

docs.title: Control plane
docs.text:
The control plane handles changes, not every application request:

  • Admin API: create/update flags, targeting rules, rollout percentage, environment.
  • Validation: type-check variations, validate operators and attributes, reject invalid or contradictory rules.
  • Persistence: store the canonical configuration and version it.
  • Audit: record who changed what, before/after values, timestamp, environment, and reason.
  • Distribution: notify SDKs that a new version exists (streaming/SSE/WebSocket) or let them poll.

docs.title: Data plane
docs.text:
Each SDK maintains a local, immutable configuration snapshot:

  1. Start with an embedded safe fallback or bootstrap configuration.
  2. Fetch the latest snapshot and wait for the provider to become ready (or explicitly accept defaults).
  3. Subscribe to change events or poll periodically.
  4. Validate a received snapshot.
  5. Atomically swap the active snapshot.
  6. Evaluate flags in memory; do not call the control plane for each evaluation.

A snapshot is better than mutating individual rules in place: readers see either the old complete version or the new complete version, never a partially updated configuration.

docs.title: 5. Data model
docs.text:
A practical model separates a flag definition from environment-specific state.

Flag
- key: string (stable, unique)
- type: BOOLEAN | STRING | NUMBER | JSON
- variations: [typed values]
- owner/team
- category: RELEASE | EXPERIMENT | OPS | ENTITLEMENT
- created_at, expires_at (optional)

EnvironmentFlag
- flag_key
- environment
- enabled
- default_variation
- rules: ordered list
- rollout: optional
- config_version

Rule
- id
- priority/order
- conditions: AND of clauses
- result: variation OR rollout

Clause
- attribute_path
- operator: EQ, IN, GT, CONTAINS, EXISTS, ...
- operand

Rollout
- targeting_key
- salt / allocation_key
- percentage per variation

Keep the rule language deliberately small. Arbitrary code in rules creates security, portability, debugging, and performance problems. Validate attribute types and support explicit behavior for missing/null attributes.

docs.title: 6. Evaluation algorithm: precedence must be explicit
docs.text:
For a boolean flag, one defensible evaluation order is:

  1. Flag disabled in this environment? Return its configured off/default variation.
  2. Explicit exclusion? Return off (or a designated safe variation).
  3. Explicit inclusion? Return the included variation.
  4. Evaluate ordered rules: the first matching rule wins.
  5. Rule's percentage rollout: choose a stable variation using the context's targeting key.
  6. Fallthrough: return the environment's default variation.

The actual order is a product decision, but it must be documented, consistent across SDKs, and testable. Explicit exclusions commonly override inclusion/rollout to make emergency controls unambiguous.

docs.title: Deterministic percentage assignment
docs.text:
Do not randomly select a user on every request. That would make one person alternate between old and new code and contaminate experiments.

Instead compute a stable bucket:

bucket = HASH(flag_key + ":" + targeting_key + ":" + allocation_salt)
         mod 10,000

enabled if bucket < percentage * 100

For a 7.5% rollout, buckets 0–749 are enabled. The same flag and targeting key map to the same bucket on every evaluation.

  • The targeting key should identify the subject consistently: user ID, account/tenant ID, or another chosen unit.
  • Include a flag-specific salt/key so different flags usually select different cohorts.
  • If related flags need the same cohort, deliberately share an allocation key.
  • Use a stable, specified hash algorithm. Changing the algorithm or salt can reshuffle users.
  • As a percentage increases, threshold-based buckets preserve the earlier cohort (e.g., 10% remains included when moving to 30%).

For multi-variation experiments, map the bucket to weighted ranges. Validate that weights sum to 100%, or define an explicit remainder policy.

docs.title: 7. Worked example: new checkout flow
docs.text:
Suppose we are rolling out checkout-v2:

  • Default: false
  • Environment: production
  • Rule 1: internal employee cohort → true
  • Rule 2: enterprise accounts in region IN → 100% true
  • Fallthrough: 5% rollout → true, otherwise false

For a request with context:

{
  "targetingKey": "user-8472",
  "accountTier": "standard",
  "region": "IN",
  "isEmployee": false
}

The employee rule doesn't match. The enterprise rule doesn't match. We evaluate the percentage rollout. Assume the deterministic bucket for checkout-v2:user-8472 is 3,412. Since 5% corresponds to buckets 0–499, the flag is false for this user.

If the rollout increases to 20%, the bucket range becomes 0–1,999. This user remains off. Another user whose bucket is 1,234 changes to on and will consistently receive the new checkout on subsequent requests.

The key is that rollout percentage is a cohort boundary, not a fresh random decision.

docs.title: 8. Operational rollout workflow
docs.text:
A flag should have an owner, category, creation date, and (for temporary flags) an expiry/removal issue.

A safer release sequence:

  1. Deploy dark: code is present but flag is off for everyone. Verify both code paths and rollback safety.
  2. Internal cohort: turn on for employees/test accounts.
  3. Small stable cohort: 1% or a carefully chosen low-risk group.
  4. Observe: compare error rate, conversion, latency, resource usage, and dependency health against baseline.
  5. Ramp: 5% → 25% → 50% → 100%, pausing at each step when metrics warrant.
  6. Rollback: disable the flag or reduce rollout; confirm propagation and that the old path is still safe.
  7. Cleanup: after full release and confidence, remove the old branch, flag config, tests that only cover the temporary toggle, and stale targeting.

For experiments, use a fixed assignment during the experiment and avoid changing the cohort allocation midway unless the experiment plan accounts for it.

docs.title: Push vs. poll
docs.text:
Approach Advantages Costs / risks Polling Simple, easy to recover after missed events Change propagation bounded by poll interval; repeated requests Push/stream Faster updates, less polling traffic Connections, reconnects, missed events, operational complexity Hybrid Push invalidation + periodic full snapshot More moving parts, often a practical balance

A push event should generally carry a version or tell the SDK to fetch the latest snapshot. The client must not apply an older version after a newer one.

docs.title: Failure policy
docs.text:
• Control-plane outage: continue using the last known good snapshot.
  • SDK not initialized: return a code-level default and expose a readiness/error signal. Do not silently pretend configuration is ready.
  • Malformed update: reject the whole snapshot; keep the previous valid one.
  • Stale snapshot: monitor age and decide per flag whether stale evaluation is acceptable. Most release flags can tolerate short staleness; a critical operational kill switch needs tighter propagation and an explicit mitigation path.
  • Network partitions: no system can guarantee instant global propagation. Define the target (e.g., 99% of connected SDKs within a chosen interval) and alert when it is violated.

For a kill switch, consider whether SDKs should receive push updates, use a shorter poll interval, and/or have a separate emergency control path. Measure the time from operator action to effective disablement.

docs.title: 10. LLD: an evaluator that is testable
docs.text:
Keep the evaluator pure: it receives a validated snapshot, flag key, and context; it returns a value plus reason. It should not fetch data or mutate state.

evaluate(flag, context):
    if flag.disabled:
        return result(flag.offVariation, DISABLED)

    if matches(flag.exclusions, context):
        return result(flag.offVariation, EXCLUDED)

    if matches(flag.inclusions, context):
        return result(flag.includedVariation, TARGETED)

    for rule in flag.rules in priority_order:
        if rule.matches(context):
            if rule.rollout exists:
                variation = deterministicBucket(rule.rollout, context.targetingKey)
                return result(variation, RULE_ROLLOUT, rule.id)
            return result(rule.variation, RULE_MATCH, rule.id)

    return result(flag.fallthrough, FALLTHROUGH)

A production result should include metadata such as flag key, config version, reason code, matched rule ID, and provider status. Avoid logging full targeting context or sensitive attributes.

Useful LLD abstractions:

  • FlagProvider: obtains/updates snapshots and reports readiness.
  • SnapshotStore: atomic read/swap of immutable configuration.
  • Evaluator: pure rule and rollout evaluation.
  • Context: typed attributes + targeting key.
  • EvaluationResult: typed value + reason + version.
  • FlagAdminService: validation, persistence, authorization, audit, publish.

Don't over-engineer a generic rule engine at first. Add operators only when real use cases require them.

docs.title: 11. Testing strategy
docs.text: Test the evaluator and distribution system separately.

docs.title: Evaluator tests
docs.text:
• disabled flag beats every targeting rule;
  • exclusion beats inclusion/rollout;
  • rule ordering is stable and first-match semantics work;
  • missing or null attributes behave as documented;
  • typed variation mismatches are rejected;
  • same flag + key yields same bucket;
  • different flags produce different cohorts unless allocation is shared;
  • increasing percentage is monotonic;
  • 0% and 100% boundaries are exact;
  • invalid weights/config fail validation.

docs.title: SDK/config tests
docs.text:
• startup fallback and readiness behavior;
  • snapshot update is atomic;
  • out-of-order versions are ignored;
  • reconnect fetches the latest full snapshot;
  • malformed config leaves last-known-good snapshot intact;
  • timeout/stale snapshot policy is followed;
  • kill-switch propagation is measured;
  • evaluation emits reason/version without PII.

docs.title: Integration and release tests
docs.text: Use contract tests for the admin API and provider. Simulate a flag update while application instances are running. Test both code paths and rollback—not just the enabled path. Verify that a flag doesn't accidentally expose a client-side-only secret or bypass authorization.

docs.title: 12. Trade-offs and design choices
docs.text:
• Local vs remote evaluation: local is fast and resilient but requires config distribution and snapshot consistency; remote centralizes evaluation but adds latency, dependency failure, and per-request cost.
  • Polling vs streaming: polling is simpler and more robust; streaming gives quicker changes but needs reconnect/version handling.
  • Simple booleans vs typed variations: booleans are easy; variants support experiments but increase validation and code complexity.
  • Static vs dynamic targeting: attribute/segment rules scale better than enormous per-user lists; direct targeting is useful for small exceptions but can become stale flag debt.
  • Fail-open vs fail-closed: feature defaults should protect service availability, but the correct fallback is feature-specific. Neither is universally correct.
  • Control plane centralization: one source of truth improves governance; regional replicas and local snapshots reduce latency and blast radius but complicate propagation.

docs.title: 13. Common pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Random assignment on every request—users flicker between variants.
  2. Targeting key missing or unstable—rollout cohort changes between sessions.
  3. Rules with unclear precedence—contradictory targeting becomes difficult to debug.
  4. Calling the flag service in the request path—availability and latency become coupled to the control plane.
  5. Treating a flag as authorization—client-controlled or stale flag values can expose protected actions.
  6. Sending PII in targeting context—privacy, compliance, and data retention risks.
  7. Never removing flags—permanent branches multiply test combinations and confuse future changes.
  8. No owner/expiry—nobody knows whether a flag is safe to delete.
  9. Testing only the new branch—rollback path may be broken.
  10. Assuming instant propagation—SDKs can be disconnected; measure and define the bound.

docs.title: 14. Interview questions
docs.text:
1. Why should feature-flag evaluation usually be local rather than a network call?
  2. How do you guarantee stable cohort assignment across requests?
  3. What changes if the targeting key is a tenant instead of a user?
  4. How do you handle a control-plane outage or invalid config update?
  5. How would you design a kill switch whose propagation must be very fast?
  6. Why is feature-flag state not an authorization mechanism?
  7. How do you avoid all flags selecting the same 5% cohort?
  8. What metrics would you watch during a rollout?
  9. What are the consistency implications of a push-based config channel?
  10. How would you reduce flag debt and avoid testing every combination of N flags?

docs.title: 15. Exercise
docs.text:
Design a feature-flag platform for an e-commerce service with 5 million daily users and 300 backend instances.

Requirements: - An operator can disable recommendations within 10 seconds. - Rollout is stable by user ID. - Rules support country, account tier, and employee targeting. - SDK evaluations add less than 1 ms in the hot path. - A flag-service outage must not break checkout. - Configuration changes are audited.

Deliver: 1. A component diagram and the control-plane/data-plane boundary. 2. The flag schema and rule precedence. 3. Your hash/bucket strategy and how you preserve cohorts during a ramp. 4. Polling/streaming choice, reconnect strategy, and version handling. 5. Fallback behavior for checkout vs. recommendations. 6. A rollout plan with the metrics and rollback thresholds you would choose. 7. Tests for the 10-second kill-switch objective and failure scenarios.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Martin Fowler — Feature Toggles (aka Feature Flags) — toggle categories, implementation and flag debt.
  • OpenFeature — Providers — provider abstraction between application SDKs and flag systems.
  • OpenFeature — Evaluation Context — context layering, targeting keys and PII considerations.
  • OpenFeature Specification — Flag Evaluation API — typed evaluation and defaults.
  • LaunchDarkly — Flag Evaluation Rules — ordered rule matching and fallthrough behavior.
  • LaunchDarkly — Deciding between flag targeting strategies — scalable attribute/segment targeting vs. individual targets.

docs.title: Requirements Engineering: Define the Problem Before Designing
docs.text: Subject: Low-Level Design & High-Level Design Level: Beginner to Intermediate Topic: Requirements discovery, analysis, specification and validation Prerequisites: None — foundational lesson Tags: system-design requirements-engineering LLD HLD NFR quality-attributes

docs.title: 1. Learning objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

  • Explain what requirements engineering is.
  • Distinguish functional requirements, quality requirements, constraints and assumptions.
  • Identify system scope and out-of-scope features.
  • Elicit requirements from a vague problem statement.
  • Convert vague requirements into measurable and testable statements.
  • Understand SLI, SLO and SLA.
  • Explain how requirements influence LLD and HLD decisions.
  • Structure requirements discussions in system design interviews.

docs.title: 2. What is requirements engineering?
docs.text:
Requirements engineering is the process of discovering, analysing, documenting, validating and managing the needs and constraints of a software system.

It converts a vague business problem into concrete expectations that can guide design, implementation and verification.

Example problem:

"Design a URL shortener."

Before designing it, clarify:

  • Who can create short URLs?
  • Are users authenticated?
  • Are custom aliases supported?
  • Can URLs expire?
  • Is analytics required?
  • What is the expected request volume?
  • What is the acceptable latency?
  • What should happen when a dependency fails?

The answers influence the system's architecture.

docs.title: Requirements-to-implementation flow
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Business Problem] --> B[Requirements Discovery]
    B --> C[Functional Requirements]
    B --> D[Quality Requirements]
    B --> E[Constraints and Assumptions]
    C --> F[System Design]
    D --> F
    E --> F
    F --> G[Implementation]
    G --> H[Verification and Validation]

A good architecture is one that satisfies the requirements within the available constraints.

docs.title: 3.1 Functional requirements
docs.text:
Functional requirements describe what the system must do.

They define observable behaviours, operations, features and interactions.

URL shortener examples:

ID Requirement FR-01 A user can submit a long URL and receive a short URL. FR-02 A visitor can use a short URL to reach the original URL. FR-03 The system returns an appropriate error for an unknown short code. FR-04 The system handles expired URLs according to the expiry policy. FR-05 The system prevents duplicate custom aliases.

A functional requirement should be specific enough to implement and test.

docs.title: 3.2 Non-functional requirements / quality attributes
docs.text:
Quality requirements describe how well the system must perform its responsibilities and the conditions under which it must operate.

Attribute Meaning Example Performance How quickly operations complete 95% of redirects complete within 100 ms Scalability Ability to handle workload growth Support an agreed peak of 5,000 redirects/second Availability Whether the service can be used Target 99.9% successful redirect availability Reliability Consistent correct operation A node failure must not corrupt URL mappings Durability Protection against data loss Acknowledged mappings survive defined failure scenarios Security Protection against misuse Authenticated creation and rate limiting Maintainability Ease of modification New link policies can be added without changing redirect semantics Observability Ability to understand system behaviour Measure latency, errors and traffic Cost efficiency Resource use relative to value Meet workload targets within the infrastructure budget

The values above are illustrative, not universal recommendations. Actual targets must be agreed with stakeholders.

Non-functional does not mean optional. A system can implement all its features and still fail because it is too slow, insecure, unreliable or expensive.

docs.title: 3.3 Constraints
docs.text:
Constraints restrict the available design choices.

Examples:

  • The backend must use Java and Spring Boot.
  • The application must run on an existing Kubernetes cluster.
  • Data must remain within a specified geographic region.
  • An existing payment provider must be used.
  • The project must fit a fixed budget.

Distinction:

  • "Must use PostgreSQL" is a technology constraint.
  • "Must support 10,000 writes per second" is a performance requirement.
  • "Must store customer data in a specified region" is a data residency constraint.

docs.title: 3.4 Assumptions
docs.text:
Assumptions are provisional beliefs used when the problem statement lacks information.

Examples:

  • URL creation requires an authenticated account.
  • Short codes are case-sensitive.
  • Analytics are not required in the first version.
  • Users access the system over HTTPS.

High-impact assumptions must be validated. A wrong assumption can invalidate an otherwise sound design.

docs.title: 3.5 Scope and out-of-scope
docs.text:
Scope determines what the current design must support.

For a basic URL shortener:

In scope - Create a short URL. - Redirect to the original URL. - Handle unknown and expired links. - Enforce custom alias uniqueness if aliases are included.

Out of scope for the initial version - Click analytics. - QR-code generation. - Team administration. - Advertising and monetisation.

Explicit scope prevents unnecessary complexity.

docs.title: 4. Requirement discovery process
docs.text:
Use this sequence in design interviews:

  1. Identify users and actors.
  2. Understand the main workflows.
  3. Define functional requirements.
  4. Define quality requirements.
  5. Identify constraints and assumptions.
  6. Establish workload and scale.
  7. Prioritise and validate.

docs.title: Users and features
docs.text:
• Are users authenticated?
  • Can anonymous users create links?
  • Are custom aliases supported?
  • Can users delete or expire links?
  • Are click analytics required?

docs.title: Workload
docs.text:
• How many URLs are created per day?
  • What is the expected redirect traffic?
  • Is redirect traffic much higher than creation traffic?
  • Are sudden traffic spikes expected?

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
• What is the acceptable redirect latency?
  • Does creation have a different latency target?
  • Are there geographic latency requirements?

docs.title: Reliability and consistency
docs.text:
• What should happen when a server fails?
  • Must a newly created URL be immediately usable?
  • Can analytics be delayed?
  • What data loss is acceptable?

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Can malicious URLs be submitted?
  • Do we need rate limits?
  • How should abuse be detected?
  • What user data must be retained or deleted?

Ask questions that could change the design. Do not turn clarification into an exhaustive questionnaire.

docs.title: 5. Convert vague requirements into measurable requirements
docs.text:
Vague requirement More precise requirement The application should be fast. 95% of redirect requests complete within 100 ms under the specified workload. The system should scale. Support 5,000 redirect requests/second at the agreed latency target. The system should be highly available. At least 99.9% of eligible redirect requests succeed over a rolling 30-day period. The application should be secure. Creation requires authentication and per-user/per-IP rate limits. The system should be reliable. Acknowledged mappings are not lost during the specified single-node failure scenario.

A measurable requirement should define:

  • Measurement location.
  • Request types included.
  • Workload and operating conditions.
  • Measurement window.
  • Success and failure criteria.

docs.title: 5.1 Quality attribute scenarios
docs.text:
The Software Engineering Institute describes quality attribute scenarios using six elements:

  1. Source: Who or what generates the event?
  2. Stimulus: What event occurs?
  3. Environment: Under what conditions?
  4. Artifact: Which component is affected?
  5. Response: What should the system do?
  6. Response measure: How is success measured?

Example: performance.

Element Description Source Visitor Stimulus Requests a short URL Environment Normal peak load Artifact Redirect service Response Resolve the code and return a redirect response Response measure 95% of eligible requests complete within 100 ms

Example: failure.

Element Description Source Infrastructure Stimulus One application instance crashes Environment Normal production traffic Artifact Redirect service Response Remaining instances continue serving requests Response measure Requests remain within agreed availability and latency targets

This converts vague quality labels into requirements that can guide architecture and testing.

docs.title: 6. SLI, SLO and SLA
docs.text:
Term Meaning Example SLI Service Level Indicator: what is measured Successful redirect request ratio SLO Service Level Objective: target for a measured service level 99.9% successful redirects over 30 days SLA Service Level Agreement: agreement that may specify consequences Contractual availability commitment with defined remedies
  • SLI tells us how the service is performing.
  • SLO tells us the expected target.
  • SLA defines the agreement and potential consequences if it is not met.

docs.title: 6.1 Why latency percentiles matter
docs.text:
Suppose request latencies are:

20 ms, 25 ms, 30 ms, 40 ms, 900 ms

Average = 203 ms.

Median = 30 ms.

The average hides the slow request.

Common metrics:

  • p50: median latency.
  • p95: 95% of requests complete at or below this latency.
  • p99: 99% of requests complete at or below this latency.
  • Throughput: operations per unit of time.
  • Error rate: proportion of requests failing under a defined error policy.

Choose metrics that represent actual user experience. Avoid blindly optimising every metric.

docs.title: 7. How requirements influence architecture
docs.text:
Requirement Possible design consequence High redirect traffic Read optimisation, caching and horizontal scaling Custom aliases must be unique Database uniqueness enforcement and concurrency-safe creation New links must be immediately usable Read-after-write consistency considerations Analytics may be delayed Asynchronous event processing may be acceptable Links can expire Expiry checks, retention policy and background cleanup Multiple geographic regions Regional deployment and replication Strict data residency Region-specific storage and processing Sensitive account data Authentication, authorisation, encryption and audit controls

A requirement does not automatically dictate a technology.

High read traffic does not automatically mean Redis. Evaluate read patterns, latency, consistency, working-set size and cost first.

docs.title: 7.1 LLD versus HLD
docs.text:
Area LLD emphasis HLD emphasis Behaviour Methods and operations System-level workflows State Object state and transitions Persistent and distributed state Correctness Invariants and business rules End-to-end correctness Concurrency Locks, races and thread safety Concurrent requests and coordination Performance Algorithmic efficiency Latency, throughput and capacity Failure Exceptions and component recovery Node, service, network and region failures Security Validation and access checks Trust boundaries and data protection

LLD and HLD use the same requirements but translate them into different levels of design.

docs.title: 8. Writing useful requirements
docs.text:
Good requirements should be:

  • Necessary.
  • Unambiguous.
  • Verifiable.
  • Feasible.
  • Traceable.
  • Consistent.
  • Prioritised.

docs.title: 8.1 MoSCoW prioritisation
docs.text:
• Must have: essential.
  • Should have: important but not essential for the first release.
  • Could have: useful if resources permit.
  • Won't have now: explicitly deferred.

Example:

Feature Priority Create short URL Must Redirect short URL Must Unknown-link handling Must Custom aliases Should Click analytics Could QR-code generation Won't have now

docs.title: 9. Common mistakes
docs.text:
1. Choosing technologies before understanding requirements.
  2. Ignoring invalid input, expiry and duplicate aliases.
  3. Using vague NFRs such as "highly scalable".
  4. Overengineering an MVP.
  5. Treating assumptions as confirmed requirements.
  6. Ignoring cost.
  7. Failing to prioritise.
  8. Not validating requirements with stakeholders.

docs.title: Basic
docs.text:
Q1. Difference between functional and non-functional requirements?

Functional requirements define capabilities and behaviour. Quality requirements define properties such as latency, availability, security and maintainability.

Follow-up: Can a system satisfy functional requirements and still fail?

Yes. It can produce correct results but be slow, insecure, unreliable or too expensive.

Q2. Difference between a constraint and a quality requirement?

A constraint restricts design choices. A quality requirement defines an expected property of the system.

Example: "Must use Java" is a technology constraint; "95% of requests must finish within 200 ms" is a performance requirement.

Q3. What is an assumption?

A provisional belief used when information is missing. It should be documented and validated.

docs.title: Intermediate
docs.text:
Q4. Why define quality requirements before architecture?

Architecture involves trade-offs. Workload, latency, reliability, security and consistency targets are necessary to evaluate design decisions.

Q5. Why might average latency be insufficient?

It hides tail latency. p95 and p99 reveal slow requests that can materially affect users.

Q6. Does high availability mean no failures?

No. It means the service meets its availability objective despite failures. Define failure scenarios, acceptable degradation and recovery expectations.

docs.title: Advanced
docs.text:
Q7. What if the interviewer asks for 100% availability?

Clarify the business meaning and measurement. Explain that absolute availability is not a realistic engineering target. Discuss failure budgets, recovery expectations, redundancy, dependency risks and cost.

Q8. What if performance and consistency requirements conflict?

Identify which operations require strong consistency and which can tolerate stale or delayed data. For example, a new URL may need immediate read-after-write visibility while analytics may be asynchronous.

Q9. How do you handle incomplete requirements?

Identify uncertainty, ask the highest-impact question, state a reasonable assumption if necessary, and document it so the design can be revised.

docs.title: 11. Practical exercise
docs.text:
Write a requirements specification for a notification system.

Potential features: - Users can receive notifications. - Support email, SMS and push. - Users manage notification preferences. - Track delivery status.

Questions:

  1. Should notifications be delivered immediately?
  2. What happens if an email provider is unavailable?
  3. Can a notification be delivered more than once?
  4. Can users unsubscribe?
  5. Are notifications ordered?
  6. How long are delivery records retained?
  7. What is the acceptable delivery delay?
  8. How many notifications might arrive in a burst?

Do not design the architecture yet. First write:

  • Actors.
  • Functional requirements.
  • Quality requirements.
  • Constraints.
  • Assumptions.
  • In-scope and out-of-scope features.
  • Workload estimates or questions.
  • Failure expectations.

docs.title: 12. Key takeaways
docs.text:
1. Understand requirements before selecting architecture.
  2. Functional requirements describe what the system does.
  3. Quality requirements describe how well it must work.
  4. Constraints restrict possible solutions.
  5. Assumptions must be documented and validated.
  6. Requirements should be measurable and testable.
  7. Quality attributes drive architectural trade-offs.
  8. LLD and HLD use the same requirements at different levels.

docs.title: 13. Knowledge check
docs.text:
1. Which requirement specifies what the system must do?
  2. Is "must use Kubernetes" a constraint or a performance requirement?
  3. Which metrics reveal slow-tail requests?
  4. What is the difference between SLI, SLO and SLA?
  5. What should you do with a high-impact unknown during a design interview?

docs.title: 14. References
docs.text:
• SEI — Reasoning About Software Quality Attributes
  • NASA Systems Engineering Handbook — Requirements Checklist
  • Google SRE Book — Service Level Objectives
  • AWS Well-Architected Framework
  • SEI — Defining Non-Functional System Qualities

docs.title: What is Scalability?
docs.text: Scalability is the ability of a system to handle increased load (users, data, traffic) without degrading performance.

docs.title: Key Metrics to Measure
docs.text:
• Throughput — requests per second
  • Latency — time per request
  • Availability — uptime percentage (e.g., 99.9%)

docs.title: Real-Life Scenario
docs.text: 🐦 Twitter: Handles ~500 million tweets per day. On a regular Tuesday, traffic is predictable. But during a World Cup final or a breaking news event, traffic spikes 10–20x. A scalable system handles this gracefully instead of crashing.

docs.title: Types of Load
docs.text: Load Type Example User growth App going viral overnight Data growth 10 years of transaction logs Computation growth ML model training on bigger datasets

docs.title: Vertical Scaling (Scale Up)
docs.text:
Add more power (CPU, RAM, disk) to an existing machine.

  • Before: [Server: 4 CPU, 16GB RAM]
  • After: [Server: 32 CPU, 128GB RAM]
  • Pros: Simple, no code changes needed
  • Cons: Hardware limits, single point of failure, expensive

docs.title: Horizontal Scaling (Scale Out)
docs.text:
Add more machines running the same service.

  • Before: [Server 1]
  • After: [Server 1] [Server 2] [Server 3] (← Load Balancer distributes traffic)
  • Pros: Nearly unlimited scale, fault-tolerant
  • Cons: Requires stateless design, more complex infrastructure

docs.title: Real-Life Scenario
docs.text:
🎬 Netflix uses horizontal scaling. When a new season of a popular show drops, they spin up hundreds of additional servers in minutes using AWS Auto Scaling. They don't just make one server bigger — they add many servers and distribute traffic via load balancers.

🚀 A small startup's database might start with vertical scaling (upgrading to a bigger RDS instance) before eventually migrating to a distributed database.

docs.title: Decision Guide
docs.text:
• Is your app stateless? → Horizontal scaling preferred
  • Single giant computation? → Vertical scaling may be simpler
  • Need 99.99% uptime? → Horizontal (no single point of failure)

docs.title: How to Think About This in an Interview
docs.text:
Don't just pick one — reason through trade-offs step by step:

  1. Step 1: Calculate the numbers
    • Current: 1,000 req/sec. Expected: 50,000 req/sec.
    • Can one machine handle 50x? (Often yes, but with a hard ceiling)
  2. Step 2: Ask about fault tolerance
    • Payment service down = $1M/minute lost → single machine is unacceptable
    • Internal metrics dashboard → one machine is fine
  3. Step 3: Ask about statelessness
    • Sessions stored in-process (RAM)? → Horizontal scaling requires redesign
    • Sessions stored in Redis? → Horizontal scaling = just add machines
  4. Step 4: Give the pragmatic answer (what interviewers love)
    • "Scale vertically first — fast, cheap, zero code change. But design stateless from day one (sessions in Redis, no local disk state) so horizontal scaling is just adding machines when you hit the ceiling."

⚠️ Interview trap: A candidate who always says "horizontal scaling" without justification sounds rehearsed. The one who says "vertical first, but here's how I'd architect for horizontal" sounds experienced.

docs.title: What is Failover?
docs.text: Failover is the automatic switch to a backup system when the primary system fails.

docs.title: Active-Passive (Cold Standby)
docs.text:
• One server handles traffic; the backup is on standby.
  • On failure, traffic switches to the passive node.
  • Downtime: A few seconds to minutes.
[Primary DB] ———(Replication)———> [Standby DB]
  (Traffic)                         (Promoted on failure)

docs.title: Active-Active (Hot Standby)
docs.text:
• Both servers handle traffic simultaneously.
  • On failure, the remaining node absorbs all traffic.
  • Downtime: Near-zero.
[Load Balancer]
           /           \
          v             v
     [DB Node A] <---> [DB Node B]
               (Sync)

docs.title: Warm Standby
docs.text: • Backup is running and synced but not serving traffic. • Faster recovery than cold standby.

docs.title: Real-Life Scenario
docs.text: Amazon RDS Multi-AZ uses Active-Passive failover. Your primary DB is in us-east-1a. If that availability zone goes down, AWS automatically promotes the standby in us-east-1b within ~60 seconds, and your application reconnects via the same DNS endpoint. Google Search uses Active-Active. Multiple data centers serve requests simultaneously. If one goes down, others absorb the traffic instantly.

docs.title: Failover vs. Fallback
docs.text:
• Failover = switching to the backup automatically
  • Fallback = switching back to the primary once recovered

docs.title: Replication Modes — What Determines Your Data Loss Window
Asynchronous Replication (Default in most systems)
docs.text:
Primary writes -> immediately confirms to app -> replicates to standby later.
- ✅ Fast writes, standby latency doesn't affect you. - ❌ Data loss window exists — standby may lag by seconds.

docs.title: Synchronous Replication
docs.text:
Primary writes -> waits for standby ACK -> confirms to app.
- ✅ Zero data loss (every write confirmed on both nodes). - ❌ Every write is as slow as the network round-trip to the standby. - ❌ If standby is unreachable, primary blocks all writes entirely.

docs.title: Semi-Synchronous (MySQL default)
docs.text: At least one replica must ACK before the primary confirms. Best balance of safety vs. speed.

docs.title: How to Think About Failover Design
docs.text:
Question 1: How much data loss is acceptable? -> defines RPO (see Section 17)
Question 2: How long can the system be down? -> defines RTO (see Section 17)
Question 3: Is a brief outage worse than stale data? -> CP vs AP decision

If RPO = 0 (zero data loss acceptable):
       -> Use synchronous replication, accept slower writes.
If RPO = seconds (small loss acceptable):
       -> Use async replication + Kafka as safety net.
       -> Kafka retains events even if DB loses them -> replay on recovery.
If RTO = seconds (must recover instantly):
       -> Active-Active (both nodes always serving traffic).
If RTO = minutes (brief downtime acceptable):
       -> Active-Passive with automated promotion.

🛠️ Real-Life: During a 2 AM PagerDuty incident on a fintech system: primary DB dies at 02:00:00, standby last synced at 01:59:54 — 6 seconds of transactions are lost forever unless Kafka retained those payment events for replay. This is why production financial systems pair async replication with a message queue.

docs.title: The Split-Brain Problem (Preview)
docs.text: When the old primary restarts after failover, two nodes both believe they are primary — causing conflicting writes and data corruption. See Section 18 for the full breakdown and how STONITH prevents it.

docs.title: What is Sharding?
docs.text:
Sharding is the process of splitting a large database into smaller pieces (shards) distributed across multiple servers.

                  [ Full User Table (100M rows) ]
                                 |
              +------------------+------------------+
              |                  |                  |
         [ Shard 1 ]        [ Shard 2 ]        [ Shard 3 ]
           (A-H)              (I-P)              (Q-Z)
                      (Sharding by last name)

docs.title: Sharding Strategies
docs.text: Strategy How It Works Example Range-based Shard by value range User IDs 1-1M -> Shard 1 Hash-based shard = hash(key) % N Distributes evenly Directory-based Lookup table maps key -> shard Flexible but adds complexity Geo-based Shard by geography US users -> US shard

docs.title: NoSQL and Sharding
docs.text:
NoSQL databases like MongoDB, Cassandra, and DynamoDB have sharding (partitioning) built in. 

# MongoDB sharding example
sh.enableSharding("ecommerce")
sh.shardCollection("ecommerce.orders", { "userId": "hashed" })

docs.title: Real-Life Scenario
docs.text:
Instagram shards its user data. With 2 billion users, no single PostgreSQL instance can hold all user data. Instagram shards by user_id, so user 1-10M lives on Shard 1, 10M-20M on Shard 2, etc. When you load someone's profile, the system knows exactly which shard to query.

WhatsApp messages are sharded by chat_id - all messages in a conversation land on the same shard, making reads fast.

docs.title: Challenges
docs.text:
• Cross-shard joins are expensive
  • Rebalancing when adding new shards
  • Hot shards when one key gets all the traffic (e.g., a celebrity's account)

docs.title: How to Think About Choosing a Shard Key
docs.text:
The shard key is the most critical architectural decision in a sharded system. Getting it wrong means redesigning storage later. 

Good shard key:
 ✅ High cardinality (many unique values -> even distribution)
 ✅ Queries mostly hit one shard (avoids cross-shard joins)
 ✅ No celebrity/viral key problem (no single value gets disproportionate traffic)

Bad shard key examples:
  ❌ Shard by country     -> 80% of users in US -> one hot shard
  ❌ Shard by created_date -> all new writes go to "today's" shard
  ❌ Shard by status      -> active/inactive -> massive imbalance

docs.title: Fixing Hot Shards
docs.text:
Scenario: WhatsApp group with 500K members - millions of reads/writes all hitting one shard (chat_id = group123). 

Fix 1: Sub-sharding the hot key
Split: group123:sub_0, group123:sub_1 ... group123:sub_N
Writes are distributed across sub-shards; reads fan-out + merge results.

Fix 2: Separate storage tier for large groups
Small chats (<1,000 members) -> sharded PostgreSQL
Large groups (>1,000 members) -> Cassandra (built for high write throughput)

Fix 3: Aggressive caching
Last 50 messages of any chat cached in Redis
90% of reads served from cache -> shard barely touched

docs.title: Consistent Hashing - Solving the Rebalancing Problem
docs.text:
See Section 20 for the full deep-dive.

Simple hash sharding breaks when nodes are added/removed: 

hash(key) % 3 -> routes to shards 0, 1, 2
Add a 4th shard:
hash(key) % 4 -> COMPLETELY different distribution
              -> almost every key now maps to the wrong shard!
              -> massive data migration required
Consistent hashing solves this by ensuring only 1/N of keys move when a node is added or removed.

docs.title: What is a Data Lake?
docs.text:
A centralized repository that stores all your raw data - structured, semi-structured, and unstructured - at any scale, in its native format. 

Data Sources                Data Lake (Raw)          Consumers
------------                ---------------          ---------
App logs       ------------> /raw/logs/     --------> BI Dashboards
DB snapshots   ------------> /raw/db-exports/ ------> ML Models
IoT sensors    ------------> /raw/iot/      --------> Data Scientists
Social media   ------------> /raw/social/   --------> Analysts

docs.title: Data Lake vs. Data Warehouse
docs.text: Feature Data Lake Data Warehouse Data format Raw (any format) Processed, structured Schema Schema-on-read Schema-on-write Storage cost Low (object storage) Higher Speed to query Slower Faster Users Data scientists Business analysts Example AWS S3 + Athena Amazon Redshift, Snowflake

docs.title: Real-Life Scenario
docs.text: Uber collects GPS pings every few seconds from millions of drivers and riders. This raw data flows into a data lake (on HDFS/S3). Data Scientists use it to train a surge pricing models, route optimization algorithms, and safety anomaly detection - all from the same raw source without tranforming it first. Netflix stores every click, play, pause, and skip event in a data lake. Engineers can re-process historical data with new algorithms to improve the recommendation engine.

docs.title: The "Data Swamp" Problem
docs.text: A data lake without governance becomes a data swamp - data nobody can find or trust. Solutions: - Data catalog (Apache Atlas, AWS Glue Catalog) - Data lineage tracking - Access controls

docs.title: OLTP vs. OLAP - Why You Must Never Run Analytics on Your Production DB
docs.text:
See Section 19 for the full deep-dive.

OLTP OLAP Full name Online Transaction Processing Online Analytical Processing Query pattern Small, fast, single-row reads/writes Massive scans over millions of rows Use case Your app (user actions, payments) Reporting, dashboards, ML Database PostgreSQL, MySQL, DynamoDB Redshift, Snowflake, BigQuery Optimized for Low latency, high write throughput High read throughput, aggregations

What happens when an analyst runs a 300M row scan on your production PostgreSQL: 

Full table scan -> consumes ALL disk I/O bandwidth
Shared locks held -> write operations queue up behind the scan
Connection pool fills -> app servers time out waiting for a connection
Users see 500 errors / infinite loading spinners

This is called: "OLAP killing OLTP"

The fix: Data flows OLTP -> Data Lake -> Data Warehouse. Analysts query the warehouse, never the production DB.

docs.title: The ETL/ELT Pipeline - Connecting Raw Data to Analytics
docs.text:
Production DB (OLTP)
     |
     v  CDC (Change Data Capture) or Nightly Export
     |
Data Lake (S3 / HDFS)                 <- Raw, unprocessed, cheap storage
     |
     v  ETL / ELT (Spark, dbt, Airflow)
     |   - Clean (nulls, format fixes, deduplication)
     |   - Join (enrich with reference data)
     |   - Aggregate (daily totals, user cohorts, funnels)
     |
Data Warehouse (Snowflake / Redshift) <- Structured, fast SQL queries
     |
     v
BI Tools (Tableau, Metabase, Looker)  -> Business dashboards

ETL vs. ELT: - ETL (Extract -> Transform -> Load): Transform before loading. Old approach, transformation happens outside the warehouse. - ELT (Extract -> Load -> Transform): Load raw first, transform inside the warehouse using SQL. Modern approach - cloud warehouses are powerful enough to handle it, and raw data is preserved for re-processing.

Real-Life: Uber's pipeline - raw GPS pings every 3 seconds -> Data Lake (HDFS/S3) -> Spark transforms -> Hive/Presto Data Warehouse -> analyst dashboards for surge pricing analysis and driver incentive reports.

docs.title: 6. ACID Compliance and the CAP Theorem
ACID Properties
docs.text: ACID guarantees reliable database transactions.

docs.title: A - Atomicity
docs.text:
A transaction is all or nothing. If one step fails, the entire transaction is rolled back.

-- Bank Transfer: atomicity ensures both happen or neither does
BEGIN TRANSACTION;
  UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 1; -- Debit Alice
  UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 500 WHERE id = 2; -- Credit Bob
COMMIT;
-- If step 2 fails, step 1 is also rolled back

docs.title: C — Consistency
docs.text:
A transaction brings the database from one valid state to another. No rules (constraints, triggers) are violated.

Example: A NOT NULL constraint on an email column ensures no transaction can leave a user profile without an email.

docs.title: I — Isolation
docs.text:
Concurrent transactions don't interfere with each other. Each transaction sees a consistent snapshot. * Transaction A: reads balance ($1000) * Transaction B: deducts $200 concurrently * Transaction A: should NOT see B's in-progress change until it commits.

Isolation levels: READ UNCOMMITTED \(\rightarrow\) READ COMMITTED \(\rightarrow\) REPEATABLE READ \(\rightarrow\) SERIALIZABLE

docs.title: D — Durability
docs.text: Once committed, data persists even if the system crashes (written to disk, WAL logs, etc.).

docs.title: CAP Theorem
docs.text:
In a distributed system, you can only guarantee 2 of these 3 properties:

         C (Consistency)
        / \
       /   \
      / PICK\
     /   2   \
    /_________\
A (Availability)  P (Partition Tolerance)
| Property | Meaning | | :--- | :--- | | Consistency | Every read gets the most recent write | | Availability | Every request receives a (non-error) response | | Partition Tolerance | System works even if network splits occur |

P is non-negotiable in distributed systems - network partitions will happen. So the real choice is CP vs. AP.

docs.title: CP Systems (Consistency + Partition Tolerance)
docs.text:
• Sacrifice availability during a partition
  • Returns an error rather than stale data
  • Examples: HBase, Zookeeper, etcd, MongoDB (default config)

docs.title: AP Systems (Availability + Partition Tolerance)
docs.text:
• Returns potentially stale data but never an error
  • Eventually consistent
  • Examples: Cassandra, DynamoDB, CouchDB, DNS

docs.title: Real-Life Scenario
docs.text: ATM withdrawals need CP behavior. You'd rather the ATM refuse a transaction ("system unavailable") than let you overdraw your account due to stale balance data. Facebook's "Like" counter uses AP behavior. If you like a post, some users might see the old count for a few seconds. That's fine - availability and speed matter more than perfect consistency.

docs.title: How to Think About CAP in an Interview
docs.text:
The most common mistake is applying CAP to the entire system instead of per operation. 

Wrong: "We use Cassandra, so our system is AP."
Right: "Our payment writes need CP - we use PostgreSQL for those.
       Our activity feed is fine with AP - we use Cassandra for that."
The one question to ask for each feature:

"What is WORSE for the user - seeing stale data, or getting an error?" 

Stale data is worse -> CP
Examples: bank balance, inventory stock count, seat booking, distributed lock

Error is worse -> AP
Examples: social feed, recommendations, like counts, search results, GPS location
The per-operation approach in a single system (e.g., ride-sharing app): 
Driver location updates (every 3 sec) -> AP (Cassandra)
Slightly stale location is fine; service must always be available

Payment processing -> CP (PostgreSQL)
Must never double-charge; errors are better than wrong charges

Surge pricing calculation -> AP (Cassandra)
A 5-second-stale price is acceptable; pricing must always respond

docs.title: 7. Using CAP to Choose a Database
Decision Framework
docs.text:
Does your app require strong consistency?
├── YES -> Is high availability critical?
│          ├── YES -> Reconsider design (try saga patterns, 2PC)
│          └── NO  -> Use CP database (PostgreSQL, HBase)
└── NO  -> Can you tolerate eventual consistency?
           ├── YES -> Use AP database (Cassandra, DynamoDB)
           └── NO  -> Rethink requirements

docs.title: Real-World Mapping
docs.text: Use Case Requirement Database Choice Reason Banking transactions Strong consistency PostgreSQL, CockroachDB CP - no stale reads Shopping cart High availability DynamoDB, Cassandra AP - cart can sync eventually Distributed locks Consistency etcd, ZooKeeper CP - must be authoritative Social media feed High availability Cassandra, DynamoDB AP - slight staleness OK Leaderboard/gaming Both? Redis + DB combo Redis for speed, DB for truth Ride-sharing location Availability + speed Cassandra AP - GPS updates every second

docs.title: Real-Life Scenario
docs.text: Amazon Shopping Cart uses AP (DynamoDB). If two devices add items simultaneously during a network glitch, both items are kept (merge conflict resolved by keeping all). This is better than failing the add. Google Spanner attempts to provide ACID + global distribution using atomic clocks (TrueTime API) - a rare CP+global system.

docs.title: What is Caching?
docs.text:
Storing frequently accessed data closer to the consumer (in faster storage like RAM) to reduce latency and backend load. 

Without Cache:                With Cache:
User -> DB (50ms)            User -> Cache (0.5ms) -> Cache Hit
                              User -> DB (50ms)     -> Cache Miss (then populate cache)

docs.title: Cache Hit vs. Cache Miss
docs.text:
• Cache Hit - data found in cache -> fast response
  • Cache Miss - data not in cache -> fetch from source, then store in cache
  • Hit Rate = hits / (hits + misses) - aim for > 90%

docs.title: Where to Cache
docs.text: Layer Example Latency CPU L1/L2/L3 Hardware cache < 1 ns In-memory (app) Java HashMap ~ 1 µs Distributed cache Redis, Memcached ~ 0.5 ms CDN CloudFront, Cloudflare ~ 10-50 ms Database query cache MySQL query cache ~ 1-5 ms

docs.title: Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading)
docs.text:
1. App checks cache
2. Cache miss -> app fetches from DB
3. App writes result to cache
4. Future requests hit cache

docs.title: Write-Through
docs.text:
1. App writes to cache AND DB simultaneously
2. Cache is always in sync
3. Slightly slower writes, but no stale data

docs.title: Write-Back (Write-Behind)
docs.text:
1. App writes to cache only
2. Cache asynchronously writes to DB later
3. Fast writes, risk of data loss if cache crashes

docs.title: Cache Invalidation on Write (Most Common Fix for Stale Data)
docs.text:
Admin updates product price -> write to DB -> DELETE product:123 from Redis
Next read -> cache miss -> fetches fresh data from DB -> re-caches it
- ✅ Simple, always correct after one miss - ✅ No risk of data loss (DB is always the source of truth) - ❌ One cache miss per update (acceptable when writes are rare) - Best for: Product prices, user profiles, config values

docs.title: How to Think About Which Pattern to Use
docs.text:
Data changes rarely + correctness critical?
└──> Cache Invalidation on Write (delete key on every update)

Data changes frequently + write speed matters?
└──> Write-Through (always write to cache + DB together)

Ultra-high write throughput, some loss acceptable?
└──> Write-Back (counters, IoT sensor data)

Data has a natural expiry window?
└──> TTL (stock prices, exchange rates, weather)

Don't know access patterns upfront?
└──> Cache-Aside / Lazy Loading (default safe choice)

Interview pattern: When asked "the website showed a stale price after an update", the answer is always Cache Invalidation on Write - not Write-Back (which is riskier) and not just TTL (which leaves stale data for minutes).

docs.title: Real-Life Scenario
docs.text: Twitter's home timeline is pre-computed and cached per user in Redis. When you open Twitter, it reads from the cache (microseconds), not from a complex SQL join across billions of tweets (seconds). The cache is updated when people follow tweets.

docs.title: Redis
docs.text:
An in-memory data structure store supporting strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams. 

# Redis basics
SET user:1001:name "Alice"         # Store
GET user:1001:name                 # Retrieve -> "Alice"
SETEX session:abc123 3600 "user_1" # Store with TTL (1 hour)
INCR page:views:home               # Atomic counter
ZADD leaderboard 9500 "Alice"      # Sorted set (leaderboards)

Use cases: Sessions, leaderboards, pub/sub, rate limiting, queues

docs.title: Memcached
docs.text:
Simple, high-performance, distributed memory caching. Only supports key-value strings. 

XMemcachedClient client = new XMemcachedClientBuilder("localhost:11211").build();
client.set("user_1001", 3600, serializedUserData);
Object result = client.get("user_1001");
Use cases: Simple object caching, when you don't need Redis's advanced features

docs.title: Redis vs. Memcached
docs.text: Feature Redis Memcached Data structures Rich (lists, sets, etc.) Key-value only Persistence Yes (RDB, AOF) No Replication Yes No Clustering Yes (Redis Cluster) Limited Pub/Sub Yes No Lua scripting Yes No

docs.title: Varnish (HTTP Cache)
docs.text:
Sits in front of your web server, caches full HTTP responses. 

Browser -> Varnish -> Web Server
           ↑ Returns cached HTML/JSON

Use cases: Caching entire API responses or web pages

docs.title: Real-Life Scenario
docs.text: Instagram uses both Redis and Memcached at massive scale. Redis handles the social graph (who follows whom) and Memcached caches serialized Python objects (user profiles, media metadata) as a last resort.

docs.title: 10. Eviction Strategies for Caching
docs.text: When a cache is full, old entries must be removed to make room for new ones. The strategy determines which entries are evicted.

docs.title: LRU — Least Recently Used
docs.text:
Evicts the entry that hasn't been accessed for the longest time. 

Cache (capacity: 3):
[A, B, C] -> Access D -> evict A (oldest) -> [B, C, D]

Best for: General-purpose caching, web sessions Used by: Redis (default policy), many CPU caches

docs.title: LFU — Least Frequently Used
docs.text:
Evicts the entry with the fewest total accesses. 

Cache: A(accessed 10x), B(accessed 2x), C(accessed 1x)
Add D -> evict C (least frequent) -> [A, B, D]

Best for: When popular items should stay forever Pitfall: New items are always at risk of eviction before they get popular

docs.title: FIFO — First In, First Out
docs.text:
Evicts the oldest inserted entry, regardless of usage.

Queue: [A, B, C] -> Add D -> evict A -> [B, C, D]

Simple but rarely optimal — a heavily used old item gets evicted unfairly.

docs.title: TTL — Time To Live
docs.text:
Each entry expires after a set duration.

jedis.setex("product:123", 300, productJson); // expires in 5 minutes

Best for: Data that becomes stale (stock prices, weather, exchange rates)

docs.title: Random Replacement
docs.text: Evicts a random entry. Surprisingly effective and CPU-cheap.

docs.title: MRU — Most Recently Used
docs.text: Evicts the most recently used entry. Counterintuitive but useful when old data is more likely to be accessed again (e.g., rotating through a dataset once).

docs.title: Summary Table
docs.text: Strategy Evicts Best For LRU Least recently accessed General purpose LFU Least frequently accessed Popularity-based caching FIFO Oldest inserted Simple queues TTL Expired entries Time-sensitive data Random Random entry Low overhead needs MRU Most recently accessed Cyclical access patterns

docs.title: Real-Life Scenario
docs.text:
Redis with maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru will automatically evict the least recently used keys when it hits its memory limit. A news website using Redis to cache articles would naturally keep today's top stories in cache (frequently accessed) while yesterday's stories are evicted.

Browser cache uses TTL: Cache-Control: max-age=86400 tells the browser to keep a CSS file for 24 hours before re-fetching.

docs.title: What is a CDN?
docs.text:
A CDN is a geographically distributed network of servers (Points of Presence / PoPs) that delivers content to users from the nearest location.

Without CDN:
User in Tokyo ------------------------------> Origin Server (New York) [200ms]

With CDN:
User in Tokyo -> CDN PoP (Tokyo) -> Origin (only on cache miss) [10ms]

docs.title: How CDNs Work
docs.text:
1. User requests https://cdn.example.com/logo.png
  2. DNS resolves to nearest CDN PoP (based on Anycast routing)
  3. CDN checks its cache -> Cache Hit -> returns immediately
  4. Cache Miss -> CDN fetches from origin, caches it, returns to user
  5. Next user in same region -> instant cache hit

docs.title: What CDNs Cache
docs.text:
• Static assets: Images, CSS, JS, fonts, videos
  • Dynamic content: Some CDNs (Cloudflare Workers, Lambda@Edge) run code at the edge
  • API responses: With appropriate cache headers

docs.title: Popular CDNs
docs.text: CDN Known For Cloudflare Security + performance, free tier AWS CloudFront Deep AWS integration Akamai Enterprise, oldest CDN Fastly Real-time purging, Varnish-based Google Cloud CDN GCP integration

docs.title: Real-Life Scenario
docs.text:
Netflix uses their own CDN called Open Connect. They place servers inside ISP data centers (Comcast, AT&T, etc.). When you stream a popular show, the data never leaves the ISP's network — it comes from a server physically near you. This is why Netflix can stream 4K to 200M+ subscribers simultaneously.

Spotify uses CDNs to distribute song files. The MP3 file for "Blinding Lights" is cached at hundreds of PoPs globally. The first person to stream it in Lagos triggers a fetch from origin; everyone after gets it from the Lagos PoP.

docs.title: CDN Cache Invalidation
docs.text:
# AWS CloudFront invalidation
aws cloudfront create-invalidation \
  --distribution-id E1234 \
  --paths "/images/*" "/css/main.css"

docs.title: What is Resiliency?
docs.text:
The ability of a system to absorb failures and recover to normal operation, minimizing impact on users.

Fragile System: Failure -> System Down -> Users affected
Resilient System: Failure -> Degraded Mode -> Auto-recover -> Users barely notice

docs.title: Key Resiliency Concepts
docs.text: Concept Definition Fault Tolerance System continues working despite component failures Graceful Degradation System offers reduced functionality instead of failing entirely Self-Healing System detects and corrects faults automatically Redundancy Duplicate components so failure of one doesn't cause outage

docs.title: Resiliency vs. Reliability vs. Availability
docs.text:
• Reliability - probability that system works correctly over time
  • Availability - percentage of time system is operational
  • Resiliency - how well system handles and recovers from failure
Availability = Uptime / (Uptime + Downtime)

99%    = ~3.65 days downtime/year
99.9%  = ~8.7 hours downtime/year
99.99% = ~52 minutes downtime/year (four nines)
99.999% = ~5 minutes downtime/year  (five nines)

docs.title: Real-Life Scenario
docs.text: During the 2021 Facebook outage, a configuration change caused all Facebook's data centers to withdraw their BGP routes. The entire system went down for ~6 hours. This was a resiliency failure — a single misconfiguration cascaded globally.

docs.title: Circuit Breaker
docs.text:
Stops calling a failing service to give it time to recover - like an electrical circuit breaker. 

States:
CLOSED    -> requests flow normally
OPEN      -> requests fail fast (no calls to broken service)
HALF-OPEN -> test if service recovered, then close or reopen

Failure threshold hit
CLOSED ------------------------> OPEN
  ^                               |
  |                               v
  |                        Timeout expires
  |                               |
  |                               v
  +--- success? ------ HALF-OPEN <-+
  |                      |
  +--- failure? ---------+

Libraries: Netflix Hystrix, Resilience4j, Polly (.NET)

docs.title: Retry with Exponential Backoff
docs.text:
public <T> T callWithRetry(Callable<T> fn, int maxRetries) throws Exception {
    for (int attempt = 0; attempt < maxRetries; attempt++) {
        try {
            return fn.call();
        } catch (TransientException e) {
            double wait = Math.pow(2, attempt) + Math.random(); // // jitter
            Thread.sleep((long)(wait * 1000));
        }
    }
    throw new MaxRetriesExceededException();
}
Jitter prevents the thundering herd problem where all retries hit the server simultaneously.

docs.title: Bulkhead Pattern
docs.text:
Isolate components so failure in one doesn't drain resources from others.

Thread Pool A (Payment Service)    -> max 20 threads
Thread Pool B (Recommendation)     -> max 10 threads
Thread Pool C (Search)             -> max 30 threads

If Recommendations floods -> only its pool is exhausted, others work fine

docs.title: How Cascading Failures Actually Happen - Thread Pool Exhaustion
docs.text:
This is the root mechanism behind most "one service took down the whole app" incidents. Interviewers want you to explain why it cascades, not just that it does.

Recommendation Service slows: 50ms -> 8 seconds response time
↓
Each in-flight request holds one app server thread open for 8 seconds
↓
100 concurrent users * 8 seconds = 800 thread-seconds consumed simultaneously
↓
App server thread pool (200 threads total) is completely exhausted
↓
New requests for Payment, Notifications, Search also need threads
↓
They queue up -> time out -> users get 500 errors
↓
Entire app appears down, even though Payment Service is perfectly healthy
The Recommendation Service didn't crash — It held threads hostage.

The three-layer defence (must be used together): 

Layer 1 - Timeout
requests.get(url, timeout=0.5) # fail fast, don't wait 8 seconds
-> Prevents threads from being held hostage

Layer 2 - Bulkhead
Separate thread pool per downstream service
-> Even if Recommendations pool fills up, Payment pool is untouched

Layer 3 - Circuit Breaker
After N failures: OPEN circuit -> return default immediately, don't even call
After timeout: HALF-OPEN -> test if service recovered
-> Stops calling a broken service, giving it time to recover

Real-Life: Amazon reported that every 100ms of extra latency costs ~1% in sales. A single slow dependency holding threads doesn't crash the system — it just slows everything down, which silently bleeds revenue. Circuit breakers + bulkheads prevent this.

docs.title: How to Think About Resiliency Design
docs.text:
For every external call your service makes, ask:
1. What happens if this call takes 10 seconds?     -> Add timeout
2. What if it fails 100 times in a row?             -> Add circuit breaker
3. What if it's slow for 1000 concurrent users?    -> Add bulkhead
4. What should users see when this service is down? -> Design fallback
   (show product page WITHOUT recommendations rather than failing entirely)

docs.title: Timeout
docs.text:
Always set timeouts on external calls. Never wait forever.

HttpClient client = HttpClient.newBuilder()
   .connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
   .build();

HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder().uri(URI.create(url)).build();
HttpResponse<String> response = client.send(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());

docs.title: Health Checks & Liveness Probes
docs.text:
# Kubernetes liveness probe
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /health
    port: 8080
  initialDelaySeconds: 30
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 3 # restart container after 3 failures

docs.title: Real-Life Scenario
docs.text: Amazon's microservices use circuit breakers extensively. If the "Recommendations" service is slow, circuit breakers trip and product pages render without recommendations rather than timing out for users. This is graceful degradation in action. AWS Auto Scaling + health checks is self-healing: if an EC2 instance fails its health check, it's terminated and replaced automatically.

docs.title: The Data Scaling Challenge
docs.text:
As applications grow, data management becomes the bottleneck: 

10K users     -> Single PostgreSQL instance (fine)
1M users      -> Add read replicas, vertical scaling
10M users     -> Sharding, caching layers needed
1B users      -> Distributed databases, specialized stores per use case

docs.title: Read Replicas
docs.text:
┌─> Read Replica 1 (read queries)
App ──> Primary DB ──> binlog replication
         ├─> Read Replica 2 (read queries)
         └─> Read Replica 3 (analytics)
  • Write goes to primary only
  • Reads distributed across replicas
  • Replication lag is a consideration (eventual consistency)

docs.title: Write Scaling
docs.text:
• Sharding (split by key)
  • CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) - separate read/write models
  • Event sourcing - store events, not state

docs.title: Polyglot Persistence
docs.text:
Use different databases for different needs:

User Profiles    -> PostgreSQL (relational, ACID)
Session Data     -> Redis (fast, ephemeral)
Product Catalog  -> Elasticsearch (full-text search)
User Activity    -> Cassandra (time-series, high write)
Images/Videos    -> S3 (object storage)
Recommendations  -> Neo4j (graph relationships)

docs.title: Real-Life Scenario
docs.text: LinkedIn uses polyglot persistence: MySQL for member profiles, Espresso (their NoSQL) for messaging, Kafka for activity streams, Voldemort for key-value serving, and Samza for stream processing.

docs.title: Object Storage
docs.text:
Stores data as objects (file + metadata + unique ID). Infinitely scalable, cheap.

Use cases: Images, videos, backups, data lake files
Examples: AWS S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage

aws s3 cp large-dataset.csv s3://my-data-lake/raw/2024/

docs.title: Distributed File Systems
docs.text:
Designed for large files, high throughput (not random access).

Examples: HDFS (Hadoop), Google File System (GFS), Ceph
Use cases: Big data processing, ML training datasets

docs.title: Distributed Block Storage
docs.text:
Replicated block devices for databases and VMs.

Examples: AWS EBS, Google Persistent Disk, Ceph RBD
Use cases: Database storage that needs low-latency random I/O

docs.title: Distributed Databases
docs.text: See sharding section. Examples: - Cassandra - wide-column, AP, peer-to-peer - CockroachDB - distributed PostgreSQL, CP - Google Bigtable - wide-column, petabyte scale - DynamoDB - managed key-value + document, AP

docs.title: Comparison Table
docs.text: Solution Best For Latency Scalability S3/Object Storage Large files, archives ~50–200ms Infinite HDFS Batch processing High throughput Petabytes Cassandra High-write time-series ~1ms Petabytes Redis Cache, sessions <1ms Tens of TB Elasticsearch Search, analytics ~5ms Petabytes

docs.title: Real-Life Scenario
docs.text:
Dropbox migrated away from S3 to their own distributed block storage called Magic Pocket. They store exabytes (1 EB = 1 million TB) of user files across custom hardware in their own data centers - saving ~75% in storage costs compared to S3.

Spotify stores ~82 million songs. Each song exists in multiple formats/bitrates. They use Google Cloud Storage (object storage) for the audio files and their own distributed metadata store for song information.

docs.title: 16. HDFS Architecture
docs.text:
What is HDFS? Hadoop Distributed File System - a distributed file system designed to store very large files (GBs to TBs) across commodity hardware.

Design principles: - Files are split into large blocks (default: 128 MB) - Each block is replicated across multiple nodes (default: 3 replicas) - Optimized for streaming reads, not random access - Write-once, read-many model

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
NameNode
    - Manages filesystem namespace
    - Tracks which blocks are on which DN
    - Stores metadata (no actual data)
                 |
                 v metadata ops
    +────────────┼────────────+
    |            |            |
    v            v            v
DataNode 1   DataNode 2   DataNode 3
Block A1     Block A2     Block A3
Block B2     Block B3     Block B1
Block C3     Block C1     Block C2
Data Nodes (store actual data blocks + replicas)

docs.title: NameNode
docs.text:
• The master that manages the filesystem tree and metadata
  • Knows which files exist, which blocks make up each file, where each block is stored
  • Single point of failure -> mitigated by Secondary NameNode or HA NameNode

docs.title: DataNodes
docs.text:
• Worker nodes that store actual data blocks
  • Periodically send heartbeats to NameNode (every 3 seconds)
  • If heartbeat stops -> NameNode marks the node as dead and re-replicates its blocks

docs.title: Secondary NameNode
docs.text:
• NOT a hot standby - it periodically merges the NameNode's edit log to reduce restart time
  • In modern Hadoop, replaced by NameNode HA with ZooKeeper

docs.title: Block Replication
docs.text:
Default replication factor = 3
Placement strategy:
  Replica 1 -> Same rack as writer
  Replica 2 -> Different rack
  Replica 3 -> Same rack as Replica 2 (different node)

This balances:
  - Write performance (local write fast)
  - Rack failure tolerance (data survives rack failure)

docs.title: Read Path
docs.text:
1. Client asks NameNode: "Where are the blocks for /data/file.csv?"
2. NameNode returns block locations sorted by proximity
3. Client reads blocks directly from the nearest DataNode
4. Client assembles the file from blocks

docs.title: Write Path
docs.text:
1. Client asks NameNode to create /data/new_file.csv
2. NameNode assigns blocks and chooses DataNodes
3. Client writes to DN1 -> DN1 pipelines to DN2 -> DN2 to DN3
4. Acknowledgment flows back: DN3 -> DN2 -> DN1 -> Client
5. Client notifies NameNode of completion

docs.title: Real-Life Scenario
docs.text: Yahoo was one of the earliest large-scale HDFS users, running clusters with tens of thousands of machines storing hundreds of petabytes of web crawl data for their search engine. Facebook ran one of the largest HDFS clusters ever - over 100 petabytes storing user data, logs, and analytics. A 1 TB log file is split into ~8,000 blocks of 128 MB, spread across thousands of DataNodes.

docs.title: HDFS vs. S3
docs.text: Feature HDFS S3 Data locality Yes (compute near data) No Latency Lower for local reads Higher Cost Hardware + ops Pay-per-use Scalability Cluster-limited Infinite Management Complex Managed Modern trend Being replaced by S3+Spark Preferred for cloud

docs.title: The Two Numbers That Define Every Failover SLA
docs.text:
Every business decision about database redundancy, backup strategy, and failover design comes down to two metrics.

Metric Full Name Question It Answers RPO Recovery Point Objective How much data loss is acceptable? RTO Recovery Time Objective How long can the system be down? 
Timeline of a DB failure:
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────> time
   [Last backup]         [DB crashes]    [Failover complete]      [System restored]
       │                      │                      │                        │
       <───────── RPO ────────>                      <────────── RTO ─────────>
          (data loss window)                             (downtime window)

docs.title: Real-Life Mapping
docs.text: Business RPO RTO Why Stock trading platform 0 seconds < 5 seconds Every second = millions in trades E-commerce checkout < 1 minute < 1 minute Lost orders, revenue impact Internal HR system 1 hour 4 hours Low urgency, people can wait Personal blog 24 hours 24 hours Some data loss is tolerable

docs.title: How RPO Drives Replication Strategy
docs.text:
RPO = 0         -> Synchronous replication (write only confirmed when standby ACKed)
                   + Active-Active setup
RPO = seconds   -> Async replication + Kafka safety net
                   (Kafka retains events even if DB loses them -> replay on recovery)
RPO = minutes   -> Periodic snapshots (RDB for Redis, pg_dump for PostgreSQL)
RPO = hours     -> Nightly backups to S3

docs.title: How RTO Drives Architecture
docs.text:
RTO < 30 seconds -> Active-Active (traffic already on both nodes)
RTO < 5 minutes  -> Active-Passive with automated failover (AWS RDS Multi-AZ)
RTO < 1 hour     -> Manual failover with runbook
RTO = hours      -> Restore from backup (acceptable for non-critical systems)

docs.title: Real-Life Scenario
docs.text:
Netflix targets RPO of near-zero and RTO of seconds using their Chaos Engineering practice (Netflix Chaos Monkey). They deliberately kill random instances in production to prove their system recovers automatically. If it doesn't, they fix it before a real outage.

A fintech startup's on-call incident: Primary PostgreSQL dies at 02:00:00. Last standby sync was 01:59:54. RPO = 6 seconds. Those 6 seconds contained 3 payment confirmations that must be replayed from Kafka or manually reconciled with the payment gateway.

docs.title: What is Split-Brain?
docs.text:
When a primary DB fails and the standby is promoted, if the old primary later comes back online, you end up with two nodes both believing they are the primary - each accepting writes independently.

02:00 -> Primary (Node A) dies
02:01 -> Node B promoted to primary, new writes start flowing in
02:15 -> Node A restarts, still thinks IT is primary

Result — Two conflicting write histories:
Node A: payment #9001 = $500 deducted from Alice  <- stale branch
Node B: payment #9001 = $200 deducted from Bob    <- correct branch
Same ID, different data -> data corruption

docs.title: Why It Happens
docs.text: In a partitioned network, both nodes may believe the other is dead (each can't reach the other), and both promote themselves. This is the classic network partition scenario in CAP.

docs.title: STONITH — "Shoot The Other Node In The Head"
docs.text:
The solution is to forcibly fence the old primary before promoting the standby:

1. Standby detects primary is unresponsive
2. Before promoting itself, standby sends a STONITH command:
   - Power off old primary via IPMI/BMC (bare metal)
   - Revoke old primary's network access via firewall rule
   - Force-stop the DB process via cloud API (AWS EC2 terminate)
3. Only after confirmed fencing -> standby promotes itself

This guarantees only ONE node can be primary at any time.

docs.title: Distributed Consensus (The Right Way)
docs.text:
Modern HA systems use distributed consensus algorithms (Raft, Paxos) so a leader is only elected when a majority of nodes agree. Tools like etcd and ZooKeeper provide this:

PostgreSQL HA with Patroni + etcd
=================================

       +--------------------+              +--------------------+
       |   Patroni Node A   |              |   Patroni Node B   |
       |  (Current Leader)  |              |  (Current Standby) |
       +---------+----------+              +---------+----------+
                 |                                   |
                 | Updates Lease                     | Watches Lease
                 v                                   v
       +--------------------------------------------------------+
       |                      etcd Cluster                      |
       |                   (Consensus Store)                    |
       +--------------------------------------------------------+

If Node A dies:
  -> etcd lease expires
  -> Node B acquires the lock (only after majority of etcd nodes agree)
  -> Node B promotes itself
  -> Node A, even if it comes back, cannot acquire the lock -> joins as replica

docs.title: Real-Life Scenario
docs.text: PostgreSQL + Patroni (used by Zalando, GitLab, Notion): Patroni uses etcd or Consul as the consensus store. When a failover happens, the old primary's Patroni agent detects it lost the etcd lock and immediately demotes itself to a replica — no STONITH needed because the old primary cooperates. Redis Sentinel uses a similar majority voting system — a new primary is only elected when the majority of sentinel processes agree the old primary is unreachable.

docs.title: The Full Picture
docs.text: Feature OLTP OLAP Full name Online Transaction Processing Online Analytical Processing Query pattern Point queries (single row by ID) Full scans, aggregations, GROUP BY Query size KB of data touched GB to TB of data scanned Latency target Milliseconds Seconds to minutes (acceptable) Concurrency Thousands of users simultaneously Dozens of analysts Write pattern Frequent, small inserts/updates Bulk loads (nightly/hourly) Index type B-tree (for row lookups) Columnar (for aggregations) Examples PostgreSQL, MySQL, DynamoDB Snowflake, Redshift, BigQuery

docs.title: Why They Can't Share Infrastructure
docs.text:
OLTP query (your app):
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = 12345;  -> touches 1 row, uses index, done in 1ms

OLAP query (analyst):
SELECT country, SUM(revenue) FROM orders WHERE created_at > '2024-01-01' GROUP BY country; -> scans 300M rows, no useful index, 20 minutes

The OLAP query: - Holds shared read locks -> blocks concurrent writes - Saturates disk I/O -> all other queries slow down - Fills connection pool -> app servers time out - Causes: user-facing 500 errors despite the DB being "up"

docs.title: Columnar Storage — Why OLAP Warehouses Are Fast
docs.text:
Traditional row storage (OLTP): 

Row 1: [id=1, name="Alice", country="US", revenue=500]
Row 2: [id=2, name="Bob", country="UK", revenue=200]

Columnar storage (OLAP): 

id column:      [1, 2, 3, 4, ...]
country column: ["US", "UK", "US", ...]  <- only this column read for GROUP BY country
revenue column: [500, 200, 300, ...]     <- only this column read for SUM(revenue)

For SUM(revenue) GROUP BY country, columnar storage reads only 2 columns instead of all columns. For a 100-column table, this is a 50x I/O reduction.

docs.title: Real-Life Scenario
docs.text: Airbnb had a critical incident early on where a data analyst ran a complex reporting query directly on their production MySQL database. It triggered a full table scan that caused a cascading slowdown — booking requests started timing out at peak travel season.
